insight.title: T. Rex Lived Closer to Humans Than Stegosaurus
insight.subtitle: Stegosaurus was already an ancient fossil long before T. Rex ever walked the Earth.
insight.notificationHook: T. Rex is closer to us than Stegosaurus

sections.text: Stegosaurus lived about 150 million years ago, while T. Rex appeared 66 million years ago. That means T. Rex is chronologically closer to the invention of the iPhone than to a live Stegosaurus.
Movies lump all dinosaurs into one big prehistoric family reunion, but their era lasted so long that these two iconic species were separated by over eighty million years of quiet evolution.
If a T. Rex went to a museum during its own era, a Stegosaurus exhibit would already qualify as ancient history—complete with millions of years of accumulated dust.
Pop culture made them roommates, but time made them strangers.

audioBrief.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. Here is everything that matters today.

First up, military tensions between the United States and Iran have entered a new phase after recent strikes, even as diplomatic efforts stall. While this unfolds overseas, it could hit your wallet through rising fuel and shipping costs. Major conflicts in the region continue to pose a threat to international trade routes and global energy security.

Meanwhile, economic growth in the United States has slowed down, pinched by persistent inflation and growing trade deficits. For everyday consumers, this squeeze could make loans and credit card debt more expensive. High inflation continues to weigh down growth across major developed economies.

Switching to tech, major American technology companies are calling on the government to support open artificial intelligence models, though some leaders warn of potential cybersecurity risks. If these open models catch on, the everyday AI tools you use could become much more accessible and transparent. It comes as tech firms race to set global standards for software development.

Looking overseas, top leaders in China are pledging targeted economic measures to revive their slowing domestic growth. For businesses operating there, this could mean lower taxes and fresh financial support. Major Asian economies are taking active steps to prevent a long-term economic slowdown.

Turning to global health, an Ebola outbreak is expanding rapidly, while an effective vaccine remains several months away. Residents in the affected areas face severe delays in accessing life-saving shots when they need them most. Medical shortages like these continue to complicate global responses to dangerous infectious diseases.

Next, recent drone strikes damaged fuel tankers near a key Egyptian energy pipeline, sparking security fears along Suez oil routes. Disruptions in this critical area mean you might see higher energy and gas prices at home. Attacks on maritime shipping remain a major threat to global energy supply chains.

In business, German automaker BMW announced plans to cut up to eight thousand jobs as it faces fierce pressure from foreign rivals. European auto industry workers now face a growing risk of layoffs as market dynamics shift. Fierce competition from Asian manufacturers is increasingly disrupting global automotive markets.

Moving to agriculture, global food authorities are warning farmers to prepare for a new era of severe weather events. Your grocery bills may rise in the coming months as extreme heat and storms damage crops around the world. Severe climate patterns are placing unprecedented stress on global food supply chains.

In consumer privacy, federal regulators are suing telehealth company Hims and Hers for allegedly sharing customer medical records with major social media platforms. That means your sensitive personal health data could end up exposed to advertisers. Governments are stepping up efforts to crack down on the commercial sharing of private health data.

On a brighter note, autonomous vehicle maker Zoox has cleared its final federal hurdle to launch a paid robotaxi service. City commuters may soon be booking driverless rides straight from a smartphone app. Autonomous vehicles are steadily moving out of testing and into everyday public transportation.

Meanwhile, new trade restrictions have blocked popular Chinese smart vacuums from entering the American market. U.S. consumers shopping for top robotic vacuums could soon see fewer choices and higher prices for home appliances. Tech rivalries between nations are directly reducing options for everyday shoppers.

And finally, astronomers have released viewing tips for this week's meteor showers, which are happening alongside a bright full moon. Stargazers may need to travel to darker areas away from city lights to catch a clear view. It is a nice reminder of how much public fascination with celestial events endures around the world.

Before we leave you, here is a thoughtful beat to carry through your day. It turns out the Tyrannosaurus rex lived closer in time to modern humans than it did to the Stegosaurus. Stegosaurus was already an ancient fossil long before T. Rex ever walked the Earth.

That is your Sift Daily Briefing for today. Have a calm and pleasant day.
